Study aim, methodology and methods: To explore patient, relatives and GP views of the GPs role during initial cancer follow-up. Qual.—Int., FG.
Results/conclusion: Patients have trust in the GP. GP require good access to specialists. Follow-up plans will improve the care and cooperation. Hospitals to initiate a stronger collaboration.

Study aim, methodology and methods: To describe the actual and expected role of a GP in the different phases of cancer. Quant.—Quest.
Results/conclusion: Patients prefer oncologists to maintain overall responsibility. Patients would like their GP to be more involved, requires better communication and collaboration.

Study aim, methodology and methods: To assess oncologists’ attitudes and beliefs regarding sharing/transitioning survivorship care. Quant.—Quest.
Results/conclusion: There is a current lack of routine sharing. Absence of formal policies and guidelines. Patient preference and loss of patient outcome data are barriers.

Study aim, methodology and methods: To understand how GPs perceive their role to cancer survivors. 38 GPs. Qual.—Int.
Results/conclusion: The majority of GPs felt follow-up care was within their role. Some GPs did not feel adequately educated about the needs of cancer survivors.

Study aim, methodology and methods: To explore GP experiences and view providing cancer follow-up and taking a greater role. Quant.—Quest.
Results/conclusion: 78% GPs felt confident in their knowledge and skills to provide follow-up care. Some GPs (42%) were more willing to take on follow-up care after 3 years

Study aim, methodology and methods: To explore GP perspectives of a shared-care programme with oncologists. Qual.—Int., FG.
Results/conclusion: GPs willing to share the care but recommended role definition, training, clinical protocols, resources and access to oncologist’s consultation.

Study aim, methodology and methods: To document information needs of breast cancer patients, GPs and oncology specialists. Qual.—FG, Int.
Results/conclusion: GPs feel ill-equipped and felt unsure of their role. The care plan made the GP feel more engaged. Guidelines gave GPs more confidence in cancer follow-up care.

Study aim, methodology and methods: To examine patient perspectives and preferences on GP roles in their cancer follow-up care. Qual.—Int.
Results/conclusion: Most patients prefer follow-up care with the specialists. Barriers identified was GP lack of expertise, limited involvement during treatment, lack of continuity of care.

Study aim, methodology and methods: To examine how women experienced the post-treatment and perceived the role of the GP. Qual.—Int.
Results/conclusion: Patients felt abandoned at the end of treatment. Patients accepted follow-up care with their GP, provided there was a close working relationship with the specialist.

Study aim, methodology and methods: To explore cancer survivors’ views on shared care: what cancer survivors need. Qual.—G.
Results/conclusion: Patients need to be at the centre of the care. Information sharing between health professionals is important. It was perceived the GPs lacked the skills for shared care.

Study aim, methodology and methods: To explore the views of cancer survivors, oncologist and GPs, about GPs involved in follow-up care. Qual.—Int.
Results/conclusion: It was important for GPs to have knowledge and an interest in cancer. It was important for the specialist to oversee the care and maintain overall responsibility.

Study aim, methodology and methods: To explore how non-English and English-speaking patients perceive care to be coordinated. Qual.—Int.
Results/conclusion: Both groups described similar barriers to care, but non-English-speaking participants described additional communication difficulties and perceived discrimination.

Study aim, methodology and methods: To examine the experiences of patients and healthcare professionals of follow-up in primary care. Qual.—Int.
Results/conclusion: There is a lack of clear policies and practices. Disparities in knowledge, understanding, processes and pathways. Unclear roles and responsibilities.

Study aim, methodology and methods: To explore views on patient suitability for long-term colorectal cancer shared care. Qual.—Int.
Results/conclusion: Stronger systems such as cancer-specific training, survivorship care protocols, shared information systems, care coordination and navigational supports are needed.

Study aim, methodology and methods: To determine the current practice and views of GPs in England about cancer survivorship care. Quant.—Quest
Results/conclusion: GPs felt that cancer follow-up care can be shared, with the specialist maintaining overall responsibility. GPs felt confident in their ability to provide follow-up care.
